summary: Proposes a richer, machine-readable set of status codes for reporting mail system errors, beyond the limited codes in SMTP and system-specific text. These codes are meant for delivery status notifications. It was replaced by RFC 3463.

eli5.summary: Instead of just saying something went wrong, a mail server can give a short code that says exactly what kind of problem happened, so computers can understand it too.

subtitle: Machine-readable codes that say exactly what went wrong with email delivery.

tldr.problem: SMTP's original error codes (roughly a dozen) are too limited and overloaded to report specific delivery problems, making it hard for mail systems to understand or fix issues.
tldr.mechanism: A new three-part code format (class.subject.detail) uses the first digit for success or failure type, the second for the problem category (addressing, mailbox, system, network, protocol, media, or security), and the third for a specific condition.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems can now report precise, machine-readable error reasons in delivery status notifications (DSNs), letting senders and systems understand exactly why a message failed. It was superseded by RFC 3463.

today: RFC 1893 was published as a Proposed Standard in January 1996 and provided significant improvements over SMTP's error code system. It was obsoleted by RFC 3463, which updated the code definitions and examples. Today, enhanced status codes remain the standard for reporting mail delivery errors.

sections.title: The Problem with SMTP Error Codes
sections.content:
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) has been reporting mail delivery problems for decades, but its error code system is limited. RFC 821 defined roughly a dozen useful codes, but each code is overloaded to mean multiple error conditions. For example, a single code covers various addressing problems without distinguishing between a bad mailbox name, a bad domain, or a syntax error.

When delivery systems need to notify a sender of a failed message through a Delivery Status Notification (DSN), this imprecision is a problem. The sending system cannot tell the user whether to fix the email address, contact the remote postmaster, or wait and retry later.

The RFC number space for SMTP codes is also nearly exhausted, leaving only 5 slots for mail system errors. If we need to add codes for MIME type conversion, security problems, and other concerns, we would run out.
sections.eli5: The old system of codes has too few slots and each slot means too many different things. Imagine traffic lights that could mean either stop, slow down, or go—drivers would get confused.

sections.title: The New Code Format
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a three-part code with the syntax class.subject.detail, where each part is a digit or digits separated by dots. For example, 5.7.1 means permanent failure, security problem, delivery not authorized.

The class field comes first and has three values:

  • 2.X.X for Success (message was delivered or accepted)
  • 4.X.X for Persistent transient failure (retry may work later)
  • 5.X.X for Permanent failure (will not resolve by retrying)

The second part, the subject, classifies what went wrong. The defined subjects are: addressing, mailbox, mail system, network and routing, protocol, message content or media, and security or policy.

The third part, the detail, gives a specific condition within that subject. For example, under addressing, detail 1 is 'bad destination mailbox address', detail 2 is 'bad destination system address', and so on.
sections.eli5: Think of the code as saying three things: is it okay or does it need a retry or is it broken? What part of the mail system had the problem? What exactly went wrong in that part?

sections.title: The Seven Problem Categories
sections.content:
Each subject code covers a class of problems. Addressing (X.1.X) reports issues with the sender or recipient address—bad syntax, the address does not exist, or the mailbox has moved. Mailbox (X.2.X) covers problems with the destination mailbox itself: it is disabled, full, or rejects messages above a certain size.

Mail System (X.3.X) indicates problems with the destination system: the system is full, not accepting messages, or lacks features needed to handle the message. Network and Routing (X.4.X) reports delivery infrastructure problems: the host did not answer, the connection failed, directory service was unavailable, or a routing loop was detected.

Protocol (X.5.X) covers failures in the mail transaction itself: invalid or out-of-sequence commands, syntax errors, too many recipients, or protocol version mismatch. Message Content or Media (X.6.X) reports problems converting or encoding the message for delivery.

Security or Policy (X.7.X) reports filtering, authentication, or cryptographic failures: sender not authorized, encryption not supported, or inability to validate the message.
sections.eli5: These seven categories cover the main reasons a message might not reach its destination: the address is wrong, the mailbox has a problem, the server is down, the network is broken, the mail software choked, the message format cannot be converted, or security got in the way.

sections.title: Design Principles and Extensibility
sections.content:
The code format is designed to be extensible. New subject and detail codes can be added over time. A mail system that encounters an unknown detail code MUST interpret it according to the subject code; a system that encounters an unknown subject MUST interpret it according to the class.

This ensures that even as new codes are defined, older clients that do not yet know about them can still extract useful information. For example, if a new code 4.3.7 is defined in the future for a mail-system problem the sender's system has never heard of, it will know from the class (4) that it is transient and should retry, and from the subject (3) that the problem is on the receiving system.

The RFC states that status codes should be registered only through standards-track documents, not invented by individual implementations. System-specific errors should be reported through other means, such as human-readable text, to keep the namespace stable and meaningful.
sections.eli5: The system was designed to work even when a mail server knows about an old code that was invented after it was made. It picks up the pattern and guesses correctly what to do.

sections.title: Use in Delivery Status Notifications
sections.content:
The primary application of enhanced status codes is in Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs), a standardized format for reporting message delivery failures and successes. When a mail system cannot deliver a message, it composes a DSN with one of these codes to explain why.

By including both a human-readable diagnostic text (for the user) and a machine-readable status code (for the system), a DSN gives both humans and software the information they need. A mail client can highlight codes that indicate the address is wrong differently from codes that mean 'try again later', and senders can choose whether to edit the address, contact the recipient by another means, or wait.

The codes are media and language independent—a mail system anywhere in the world uses the same codes, whether its native language is English, Japanese, or Arabic, making the system suitable for global email infrastructure.
sections.eli5: When a message bounces, the mail server sends back a bounce message with both a human-friendly explanation and a code. The code tells the mail software whether to suggest trying again, changing the address, or giving up.

viz.caption: Examples of Enhanced Status Codes by Class

items.label: Destination Address Valid
items.desc: Success: the address was valid and delivery succeeded.

items.label: Transient Addressing Error
items.desc: Transient: the mailbox address does not exist (for now).

items.label: No Answer from Host
items.desc: Transient: the mail server did not respond or was busy.

items.label: Bad Destination Mailbox
items.desc: Permanent: the mailbox address does not exist.

items.label: Mailbox Full
items.desc: Permanent: the recipient's mailbox has reached its quota.

items.label: Delivery Not Authorized
items.desc: Permanent: the sender is not allowed to send to this address.
